questions.prompt: For \(\dot{x} = f(x) + g(x) u\) with \(g(x) \neq 0\), the input that leaves \(\dot{x} = v\) is
options: \(u = (v - f(x))/g(x)\), an identity along those trajectories
the Jacobian of \(f\) at an equilibrium, with \(u\) left unchanged
\(u = v\), ignoring \(f\) and \(g\)
\(u = f(x) g(x)\), a product instead of a quotient
questions.explanation: Substitute and the \(f\) terms cancel, leaving \(v\), wherever \(g\) is nonzero. The Jacobian is a different, local approximation. Setting \(u = v\) leaves \(f + g v\). The product \(f g\) does not cancel \(f\).

questions.prompt: At \(x = 3\), \(f(x) = x^2\) and \(g(x) = 2\). The input that holds \(\dot{x} = 0\) is
questions.explanation: \(u = (0 - 9)/2 = -4.5\). The sign error \((0+9)/2 = 4.5\) adds \(f\) instead of cancelling it. Dividing by \(x\) instead of by \(g\) gives \(-3\). Reporting \(f = 9\) reports the drift, not the input.

questions.figure_alt: One arrow from the origin into the first quadrant.

questions.prompt: \(f(x) = 8\), \(g(x) = 4\), and the new input is \(v = -8\). The cancelling command is
questions.explanation: \(u = (-8 - 8)/4 = -4\). Cancelling only \(f\) and ignoring \(v\) gives \(-2\). Using \(v - f\) without dividing gives \(-16\). The positive quotient \(4\) adds the two terms before dividing.
questions.figure_alt: A smooth rise toward a steady level.

questions.prompt: Write the scalar input that turns \(\dot{x} = f + g u\) into \(\dot{x} = v\), in the names \(v\), \(f\), and \(g\).
questions.explanation: Solving \(f + g u = v\) for \(u\) gives \((v - f)/g\). The form \((v + f)/g\) doubles the drift instead of removing it. The form \(v - f\) forgets to divide by the input coefficient. The form \(v/g\) leaves \(f\) in the dynamics.

questions.prompt: At a state where \(f = 1\) and \(g = 0.5\), the new input is \(v = -2\). The command is
questions.explanation: \(u = (-2 - 1)/0.5 = -6\). Dividing by \(1\) instead of by \(g\) gives \(-3\). The sign error \((-2+1)/0.5 = -2\) does not cancel \(f\). Reporting \(g = 0.5\) reports the coefficient that must stay nonzero, not the command.

questions.figure_alt: One arrow from the origin into the first quadrant.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order you would linearize a scalar plant by feedback.
questions.explanation: You cannot cancel a vector field you have not written down. The division is illegal where \(g\) vanishes, so that check precedes the formula. The outer gain is designed on the linear system you just built, and the last check is where that identity holds. Designing \(v\) before the cancellation has no linear plant to place.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>the pole assigned after cancellation</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="92" y2="90"/><line x1="120" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="101" y1="85" x2="111" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="101" y1="95" x2="111" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: One cross on the negative real axis.
steps: Write the dynamics as f of x plus g of x times u.
Check that g of x is nonzero on the region you will use.
Choose u so that f plus g u equals the new input v.
Design v as a linear state feedback.
Confirm that the closed loop is that linear system on the region where g stayed nonzero.

questions.prompt: A scalar plant is being rewritten by an input map. One step is wrong.
questions.explanation: The Jacobian is a first-order approximation at one point. The cancellation is an equality along trajectories, including far from any chosen equilibrium, until \(g\) hits zero. The other steps are that identity and the linear design that sits on top of it.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>the pole assigned after cancellation</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="92" y2="90"/><line x1="120" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="101" y1="85" x2="111" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="101" y1="95" x2="111" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: One cross on the negative real axis.
steps: The law \(u = (v - f(x))/g(x)\) is an identity wherever \(g(x)\) is nonzero.
After that substitution the system is \(\dot{x} = v\), not a remainder term.
This is the Jacobian linearization, so it is valid only in a small ball around one equilibrium.
The outer choice \(v = -k x\) then places the pole of that linear system.
reasons: The Jacobian is a local approximation. This cancellation is an identity wherever g is nonzero, not a small-ball model.
Feedback linearization is valid only at the equilibrium where f is zero.
The outer gain v is not allowed to be linear.

questions.prompt: The cancellation formula is undefined when
options: \(f(x)\) is larger than \(1\)
the outer gain is negative
\(v\) is chosen as \(-kx\)
questions.explanation: The formula divides by \(g(x)\). A large drift is legal and is exactly what gets cancelled. A negative outer gain is an ordinary stable choice. Setting \(v = -kx\) is the linear design, not a singularity.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a state at which the input coefficient is checked</title><line x1="46" y1="161.7" x2="250" y2="161.7"/><polygon points="250,161.7 243.6,164.4 243.6,159" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="60.1" y1="176" x2="60.1" y2="28"/><polygon points="60.1,28 62.8,34.4 57.3,34.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="248" y="175.7" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="66.1" y="30" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="60.1" y1="161.7" x2="235.9" y2="42.3"/><polygon points="235.9,42.3 232.1,48.2 229.1,43.7" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="243.9" y="34.3" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: One arrow from the origin into the first quadrant.

options: The cancellation is exact on the set where \(g(x)\) is nonzero.
The outer loop can be an ordinary linear state feedback in \(v\).
The construction only replaces \(f\) by its Jacobian.
A zero of \(g\) can be ignored by skipping the division.
questions.explanation: Exactness is the point of the identity, and the outer design is linear by construction. The Jacobian is the other skill. A zero of \(g\) is where this law stops, not a point you skip.

questions.prompt: At \(x = 1.5\), \(f(x) = 4.5\) and \(g(x) = 1.5\). The command that enforces \(\dot{x} = -2x\) is
questions.explanation: The target derivative is \(-2 \times 1.5 = -3\), so \(u = (-3 - 4.5)/1.5 = -5\). Using \(v = -2\) instead of \(v = -2x\) gives \((-2-4.5)/1.5 = -4.333\). Cancelling \(f\) only, with \(v = 0\), gives \(-3\). Reporting \(g = 1.5\) reports the coefficient.
questions.figure_alt: A smooth rise toward a steady level.

questions.prompt: \(g(x)\) changes sign across the region you care about, so one cancellation law cannot cover it. A practical substitute is
options: the Jacobian at a single equilibrium, used globally
setting \(g\) to \(1\) everywhere
several linear designs, interpolated from a measured operating condition
deleting \(f\) from the model
questions.explanation: Where the cancellation is singular or changes character, designers often fall back on linear models at several points and blend the gains with a measurement. One Jacobian is local. Setting \(g = 1\) or deleting \(f\) invents a different plant.

questions.prompt: The cancelling command demanded by the formula lies past the actuator limit. The design that can refuse that command is
options: a larger outer gain, which reduces the required input
the Jacobian, which never asks for a large input
ignoring \(g(x)\) in the formula
a finite-horizon problem whose constraints include the actuator limit
questions.explanation: A larger outer gain usually asks for more input, not less. The Jacobian is an approximation and does not enforce a limit. Dropping \(g\) destroys the cancellation. A constrained horizon can mark the illegal inputs as infeasible and pick a legal one.
questions.figure_alt: A smooth rise toward a steady level.
